Restriction of dietary protein in- take is a mainstay of the treatment of hepatic encephalopathy, but care is required to avoid malnutrition (see p.1697). Inflammatory bowel disease. In inflammatory bowel diseas- es (p.1697) dietary modification or supplementation may often be necessary to maintain the nutritional status of the patient. Spe- cific nutritional problems include protein deficiency, fluid and electrolyte depletion, iron deficiency, and deficiencies of certain minerals, vitamins and trace elements, such as magnesium, cal- cium and vitamin D, vitamin K, and folic acid.1,2 Supplementa- tion may be oral, nasogastric, or parenteral. In general, although they are considered to have equal efficacy,3 enteral feeding is preferred to parenteral nutrition. The latter is generally reserved for those who cannot tolerate the enteral route, for perioperative use, or for specific clinical circumstances such as bowel obstruc- tion or perforation.4,5 Improvement in nutritional status, elimination of dietary anti- gens, down-regulation of inflammatory cytokines or up-regula- tion of anti-inflammatory cytokines, or alteration in bacterial flo- ra are also possible mechanisms whereby nutritional therapy may exert a therapeutic effect in inflammatory bowel disease.5-7 Although controversial as primary therapy, enteral feeding, par- ticularly with elemental diets, has been shown to be effective in the treatment of active Crohn’s disease,8 but probably less effec- tive than corticosteroids.9-11 It may also have some benefit in maintaining remission.12 There are beneficial effects in children with growth failure, which is exacerbated by corticosteroids,13,14 and some consider enteral nutrition the first choice of manage- ment in paediatric patients with Crohn’s disease.3 Combining an elemental diet with low-dose corticosteroids has also been sug- gested as a therapeutic approach in children, although it is as yet untested.14 Adult patients with Crohn’s disease who are consid- ered candidates for enteral nutrition include those on potentially high cumulative corticosteroid doses, or who are corticosteroid- refractory or corticosteroid-intolerant, or those at high risk for osteoporosis.5 Data are considered insufficient to assess the effica
